lesson.title: How Much Change It Takes to Notice a Change
lesson.summary: The difference threshold, or just noticeable difference, is the smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect, extending the logic of absolute threshold from simple detection to detecting change.
lesson.body:
Absolute Threshold answers the question of how intense a stimulus must be before it can be detected at all. The difference threshold asks a related but distinct question: once a stimulus is already detectable, how much does it have to change before that change itself becomes noticeable. Psychologists also call this the just noticeable difference, often abbreviated JND, and like the absolute threshold, it is defined statistically rather than as a fixed cutoff. The just noticeable difference is the smallest difference between two stimuli that a person can detect fifty percent of the time, which means that on some trials a person notices a given change and on other trials, at the exact same magnitude of change, they do not.

Consider a simple illustrative scenario. Imagine holding a ten pound weight and having a small amount of weight added to it. If only a fraction of an ounce is added, almost no one would notice a difference. Add a full pound, and most people would immediately notice. Somewhere between those two extremes lies each individual's just noticeable difference for that starting weight, the smallest addition they can reliably detect. The same logic applies across every sense: how much must a light dim before the change registers, how much must a tone rise in pitch before it sounds different, how much salt must be added to a dish before a diner can tell.

What makes the difference threshold psychologically interesting, rather than just a variation on absolute threshold, is that it reveals how sensation works comparatively rather than absolutely. The nervous system did not evolve to report exact physical measurements the way a scale or thermometer does. It evolved to detect meaningful change against a baseline, since change usually signals something worth attending to, a predator moving, food spoiling, a voice becoming urgent, while a constant, unchanging stimulus usually does not require continued vigilance. Measuring the just noticeable difference is therefore a way of quantifying how finely tuned that change detecting system is for a given sense and a given starting intensity.

Just as absolute threshold required careful experimental methodology to measure, so does the difference threshold. Researchers present pairs of stimuli that differ by carefully controlled amounts and record how often participants correctly detect a difference, building a curve rather than relying on a single self report. This careful, repeated measurement approach revealed a striking regularity: the size of the just noticeable difference is not constant in absolute terms but scales with the intensity of the original stimulus, a pattern formalized as Weber's Law, which the difference threshold directly sets up.

This proportional pattern also explains something that a purely absolute view of sensation could never account for: why the same objective change in a stimulus can feel dramatic in one setting and go completely unnoticed in another, simply because the baseline against which it is being compared is different. A single extra pebble tossed onto a nearly empty scale is obvious, while the same pebble tossed onto a scale already loaded with heavy stones disappears into the noise, even though the physical weight added is identical in both cases.
